definition.text: A commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems.

facts.text: It typically covers air and water pollution, waste, ecosystem management, biodiversity, natural resources and endangered species.
It aims to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people.
In 1863 the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate after harmful chemical releases caused health problems.
Government involvement is often justified by market failures such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons.
Its effectiveness is judged by how far it reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.
Pollution of air and water tends to spur action more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems.

definition.text: The main families of tools governments use to carry out environmental policy: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion.

facts.text: Regulation sets rules, often backed by law, that ban, require or limit behaviour, such as pollution limits or bans on hazardous substances.
Critics call regulation a top-down 'command and control' approach because it leaves little choice in how goals are met.
Economic instruments use incentives: taxes, fees, subsidies, and markets for trading rights in pollutants or resources such as SO2, CO2, water and fishing quotas.
Economic instruments assume people act mainly from rational self-interest, a premise that decision-making studies cast doubt on.
Normative or 'hortatory' instruments rely on persuasion and information, such as awareness campaigns and voluntary agreements with businesses.

title: Choosing between policy instruments

definition.text: The debate over whether regulation, taxes, tradable permits or other tools work best for a given environmental problem.

facts.text: Market instruments are often promoted as a more efficient, cost-effective alternative to regulation.
Many analysts argue regulation, incentives, market instruments, taxes and subsidies can achieve the same results.
Kemp and Pontoglio found no evidence that market-based approaches are better for eco-innovation, and some evidence that regulation spurs more radical innovation.
Hahn called the performance of economic instruments 'not very impressive', and Tietenberg concluded they are 'no panacea'.
Instruments differ in how costs and benefits are shared, so distributional, ethical and political aspects matter as well as efficiency.
Tradeable permits handed to resource users are generally preferred by affected industries, which helps explain their popularity since the rise of neoliberalism.

related: Command and control versus economic incentives
contested_note: Analysts disagree whether market instruments are more efficient and innovation-friendly than regulation, or simply distribute costs differently.

title: Policy mix

definition.text: A combination of several policy instruments used together; in macroeconomics, the combination of a country's monetary and fiscal policy.

facts.text: Environmental problems have many aspects, so several instruments may be needed together.
Measures should be designed not to undermine each other, since overlapping policies add unnecessary administrative costs.
In the macroeconomic sense, monetary policy is set by the central bank and fiscal policy by the government.

notes: The seed page is about the monetary/fiscal policy mix; the environmental sense comes from Environmental policy § Comparison of instruments.

definition.text: The academic study of how environmental policies are made, how well they work and how they could be improved.

facts.text: The analycentric or rational approach uses mainly quantitative methods to find the most cost-effective solution, favouring tools such as cost-benefit analysis, taxes and tradable permits.
The policy process approach stresses politics and power, tracing steps from agenda setting through implementation to evaluation.
The meta-policy approach studies how institutions, culture, economic systems and discourses shape policymaking.

definition.text: The idea that policies in every area should take account of their effects on the environment and on other areas.

facts.text: It has been discussed since the 1980s as policy mainstreaming, policy coordination and holistic governance.

definition.text: The principle that a person gets the most from a budget by spending so that the extra satisfaction per unit of money is equal across all goods.

facts.text: It is named after Hermann Heinrich Gossen (1810–1858).
If the last unit of money spent on one good bought less extra satisfaction than it could have on another, the person would do better to switch.
Formally it follows from maximizing utility under a budget constraint with Lagrange multipliers.

title: Implicit carbon price

definition.text: A cost placed on greenhouse gas emissions indirectly, by measures that change the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself.

facts.text: Examples are fuel taxes aimed at local pollution and removing fossil fuel subsidies.
Explicit carbon prices, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading, target emissions directly; implicit and explicit together make the effective carbon price.
Fuel taxes are positive implicit prices, while fossil fuel subsidies are negative ones because they make emitting cheaper.
Implicit prices are more common worldwide: almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing.
They spread more easily because they tackle local problems, need less administrative capacity and face less political opposition.
The EU's border carbon adjustment counts only explicit prices, while a proposed US version would include implicit ones.

notes: Sentence 03d533360eb9 notes opinions differ on what counts as an implicit carbon price; definitional, not a factual dispute.

definition.text: The idea that when one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it.

facts.text: John Hicks first proposed it in 1932 in The Theory of Wages.
It is often illustrated by higher wages encouraging labour-saving inventions, and has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency.
Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption.
After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s.
In farming, when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that substitute more abundant inputs.
The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it does not include induced technological change.
